item.title: Finance Pulse - Nov 9, 2026
item.description:
I now have comprehensive, fresh data across all required domains. Here is today's Finance Pulse briefing for November 9, 2026.
---
## Finance Pulse | Monday, November 9, 2026
**Bottom line: Tomorrow's October CPI print is the week's dominant macro event, arriving without a year-over-year comparison due to last year's government-shutdown data gap -- a structurally unique release that makes month-over-month reads the only honest signal for a December hike decision; the Basel III Endgame is in its post-comment-period limbo with finalization still pending but capital relief of roughly $87.7 billion locked in by design; and the OCC's brand-new supervisory AI framework shifts agentic finance deployments at banks from a governance aspiration to an exam-ready obligation.**
---
### Top Takeaways
1. The October CPI drops tomorrow, November tenth, and cannot produce a year-over-year number. BLS will suppress the annual rate because October 2025 index levels were never published during last year's government shutdown. Month-over-month is all CFOs get, and Deutsche Bank economists are penciling in zero point two zero percent headline and zero point two zero percent core.
2. December hike conviction has hardened further over the weekend. OIS pricing stands at seventy-six percent as of November eighth; Kalshi and Polymarket converge at seventy-six to seventy-eight percent; and Commerzbank Research published a fresh note this morning reinforcing their call for a twenty-five basis point move on December ninth.
3. The Basel III re-proposal comment period closed June eighteenth and no final rule has been issued. The wait now is the dominant capital planning uncertainty for every Category I through IV bank.
4. The OCC published a formal supervisory framework for bank AI use just five days ago, specifically covering agentic AI in normal course business activities -- a first from a federal bank regulator and a direct trigger for finance governance investment.
5. First Horizon executed a four-point-five billion dollar mortgage portfolio sale that closed in late October and is guiding a four percent EPS lift, with the explicit stated mechanism being wholesale funding paydown and securities reinvestment -- a live case study in balance-sheet restructuring as a margin lever entering Q4.
---
### Three Key Themes
**Theme 1 (New): The CPI data gap as a CFO planning wedge.** Because October 2025 CPI index levels were suppressed during the government shutdown, tomorrow's Bureau of Labor Statistics release will not produce an annual inflation rate. This is not a minor technical footnote. It means the December FOMC decision, the most consequential rate-path event for bank NIM guidance in 2026, will be calibrated against an incomplete inflation signal. CFOs building Q4 and 2027 planning assumptions cannot rely on year-over-year CPI normalization this cycle.
**Theme 2 (Evolving): Wholesale funding reduction as the active NIM lever in Q4.** Prior episodes covered NIM bifurcation at the Q3 earnings level. What is new today is the operational specificity: banks across the size spectrum are actively paying down brokered and FHLB funding using balance-sheet restructuring proceeds rather than waiting for organic deposit growth to close the gap. First Horizon's mortgage sale is the freshest named example, but Mercantile Bank reduced brokered deposits by one hundred ten million while growing local deposits at an annualized eleven-point-four percent pace through September. The pattern is consistent and actionable for Q4 treasury planning.
**Theme 3 (New): The OCC agentic AI supervisory framework shifts the governance timeline.** Published November fourth, this is the first federal banking regulator to issue a supervisory framework specifically covering agentic AI in normal business activities. It places AI agent inventory, oversight design, and human-in-the-loop requirements squarely on the examiner checklist. Banks with active agentic finance pilots now face an examination posture, not just a best-practice one.
---
### Banking Finance-Function Metrics
**NIM and Deposit Dynamics:** The Q3 earnings cycle established the direction; the Q4 question is execution. Metropolitan Commercial Bank, whose Q3 NIM came in at four point three six percent, is guiding Q4 at four point one five to four point two zero percent explicitly conditioned on a December twenty-five basis point hike. Banc of California narrowed its Q4 NIM guidance to three point three five to three point four zero percent and held its pretax pre-provision income outlook at one hundred twenty-five to one hundred thirty million. Bank of Hawaii disclosed that more than fifty percent of its certificates of deposit will mature within three months at an average rate of approximately two point ninety percent, and management expects them to renew at around three percent, only modestly widening CD costs.
**Wholesale Funding Reduction as the Q4 Lever:** Mercantile Bank grew local deposits by four hundred thirty-eight million through the first nine months of 2026 while cutting brokered deposits by one hundred ten million; wholesale funds fell to roughly five percent of total funds from eight percent at year-end twenty-twenty-five. First Horizon, whose four-point-five billion dollar mortgage sale closed in late October, expects the EPS benefit to come largely through paying down wholesale funding and reinvesting proceeds in securities.
**Deposit Mix and Cost:** Analysis of super-regional deposit profiles confirms that for deposit-rich institutions the strategic focus should shift to marginal funding cost rather than chasing every incremental balance; total industry deposits reached nineteen-point-five trillion dollars at commercial banks by February twenty-twenty-six.
---
### Regulatory Radar
**Basel III Endgame -- Post-Comment Limbo:** The agencies' public comment period closed on June eighteenth, twenty-twenty-six, and no specific effective date has been set for the final rule; finalization remains pending. The March twenty-twenty-six re-proposal, which reversed course from the original twenty-twenty-three framework, delivers net capital relief of approximately eighty-seven-point-seven billion dollars relative to the earlier proposal, with finalization expected in late twenty-twenty-six and implementation in twenty-twenty-seven. Under the agencies' own estimates, CET1 requirements would fall by roughly four-point-eight percent for the largest global systemically important banks and approximately five-point-two percent for regional banks in Category III and IV.
**OCC AI Supervisory Framework (Breaking):** The OCC published a supervisory framework designed to support examiners when evaluating banks' use of artificial intelligence and agentic AI in normal course business activities. The OCC highlighted innovation opportunities, noting that banks are now exploring generative and agentic AI, while RSA Security's CEO emphasized that as bank employees deploy AI agents, the bank's task is to track the agents, identify those handling higher-risk work, and confirm the right human oversight is in place.
**SR 26-2 Model Risk Governance:** US Federal SR 26-2, effective April seventeenth, twenty-twenty-six, replaces SR 11-7 as the governing standard for AI and machine learning model risk in banking, expanding coverage to generative AI systems used in decision support and operational workflows and creating new model inventory, validation, and documentation requirements for every CFO at a financial institution.
---
### AI in Finance
**What Is Actually Deployed Versus Marketed:**
The vendor landscape has shifted from announcement to general availability claims, but banks should demand precision. Anaplan announced the Agentic Enterprise on June thirtieth with CFO-office agents due in October, though it had not confirmed general availability as of early November; Workday introduced Adaptive Decision Intelligence on May twenty-seventh for early adopters and extended it to Financials customers in October twenty-twenty-six. Anaplan's Agentic Enterprise deploys skills-based agents covering FP&A, treasury, controllership, and procurement on Amazon Bedrock.
Datarails, in twenty-twenty-six, introduced AI finance agents for strategy, planning, and reporting; in March twenty-twenty-six it also launched FinanceOS, described as a governed foundation connecting financial data, business logic, workflows, applications, and AI across the office of the CFO.
**The BCG Deployment Benchmark:** BCG data show that as much as eighty percent of FP&A work is still spent extracting and packaging data and performing simple calculations; agentic AI will move finance teams from producing reports to interpreting performance and advising the business. In one documented deployment, a finance insight agent automated more than ninety percent of business intelligence work in nine months -- work that previously took three years.
**CFO Budget Signal:** Fifty-four percent of CFOs are planning agentic deployments as a twenty-twenty-six transformation priority, specifically systems that autonomously trigger reforecasts, process payments within policy, and surface risk signals without human initiation. CFOs now allocate about a quarter of their AI budgets specifically to agentic projects.
**The OCC Governance Consequence:** The new OCC supervisory framework means that every agentic FP&A pilot inside a bank, regardless of whether it was purchased as a product feature inside Workday, Anaplan, or a point solution, now needs to be inventoried and defensible under examination. This is a demand accelerator for governance tooling and a brake on undocumented pilots. Banks buying agentic FP&A tools in Q4 and into twenty-twenty-seven should expect procurement conversations to include audit trails, model risk documentation under SR 26-2, and human override design as standard contract requirements.
---
### CFO Agenda, FP&A, and Transformation Signals
**The CPI Data Gap as a Planning Forcing Function:** A CFO cannot model a year-over-year inflation trajectory from tomorrow's release. The practical consequence is that December hike scenario planning must run on month-over-month velocity and Fed speaker signals rather than the annual CPI anchor that typically feeds budget rate assumptions. Deutsche Bank notes the market pivots this week from payrolls toward October CPI and PPI, with PPI due Friday as well. Natixis chief US economist Christopher Hodge writes that with inflation sticky above target and the labor market stable, another hike will be warranted in December.
**Finance Transformation Demand Forces Active This Week:**
- Regulatory rebuild: Basel finalization pending, SR 26-2 live, OCC AI framework published -- all three create concurrent documentation and system requirements that manual finance teams cannot absorb. - Cost-versus-workload squeeze: eighty percent of FP&A effort is still data packaging, and a December hike would add a third rate-scenario planning cycle in four months. - AI maturation and buying patterns: the evidence is that agentic finance is moving from pilot to procurement, with CFOs concentrating roughly a quarter of AI spend on agentic projects. Banks at earlier stages are now entering a catch-up window. - Deposit and funding economics: the wholesale-to-core deposit rotation visible across reported banks signals a treasury workload surge in Q4 -- hedge restructuring, FHLB repayment modeling, and CD rollover analysis -- all candidates for automation.
---
### Contrarian Insight
The consensus framing treats the CPI data gap as a nuisance. The more useful framing for a bank CFO is that it is a hidden planning gift. Because the BLS cannot publish an annual rate tomorrow, the December FOMC decision will be forced to weight real-time labor and activity data more heavily relative to the inflation print than in any prior cycle. That shifts the risk weighting back toward the jobs market -- where October's one hundred sixty-five thousand print was already the dominant upside surprise. Banks that have been anchoring December hike scenarios to a presumed CPI softening should revisit: the absence of an annual CPI number does not reduce the probability of a hike; it removes one of the few data points that could have argued against it.
---
### Client Conversation Hooks
1. **The CPI data gap question:** "Your CFO's December hike assumption is probably built on a CPI trajectory. Tomorrow's report will not publish a year-over-year rate because of the twenty-twenty-five government shutdown. How is your planning team adjusting its December scenario weights when the inflation anchor goes dark?"
2. **The OCC agentic AI examination posture:** "The OCC just published its first supervisory framework for agentic AI in bank operations. If your finance team has any AI agents running in FP&A, close, or treasury -- even as a vendor-embedded feature -- those are now examinable. Do you have an agent inventory and human override design ready for an examiner conversation?"
3. **The wholesale funding paydown playbook:** "First Horizon and Mercantile are both using non-core asset sales and organic deposit growth to systematically pay down brokered and FHLB funding before year-end. Is your treasury function running a similar optimization, and does your finance system give you the scenario modeling to know what a dollar of wholesale paydown is worth to NIM under a December hike versus a hold?"

The March twenty-twenty-six re-proposal, which reversed course from the original twenty-twenty-three framework, delivers net capital relief of approximately eighty-seven-point-seven billion dollars relative to the earlier proposal, with finalization expected in late twenty-twenty-six and implementation in twenty-twenty-seven. Under the agencies' own estimates, CET1 requirements would fall by roughly four-point-eight percent for the largest global systemically important banks and approximately five-point-two percent for regional banks in Category III and IV.
**OCC AI Supervisory Framework (Breaking):** The OCC published a supervisory framework designed to support examiners when evaluating banks' use of artificial intelligence and agentic AI in normal course business activities. The OCC highlighted innovation opportunities, noting that banks are now exploring generative and agentic AI, while RSA Security's CEO emphasized that as bank employees deploy AI agents, the bank's task is to track the agents, identify those handling higher-risk work, and confirm the right human oversight is in place.
**SR 26-2 Model Risk Governance:** US Federal SR 26-2, effective April seventeenth, twenty-twenty-six, replaces SR 11-7 as the governing standard for AI and machine learning model risk in banking, expanding coverage to generative AI systems used in decision support and operational workflows and creating new model inventory, validation, and documentation requirements for every CFO at a financial institution.
---
### AI in Finance
**What Is Actually Deployed Versus Marketed:**
The vendor landscape has shifted from announcement to general availability claims, but banks should demand precision. Anaplan announced the Agentic Enterprise on June thirtieth with CFO-office agents due in October, though it had not confirmed general availability as of early November; Workday introduced Adaptive Decision Intelligence on May twenty-seventh for early adopters and extended it to Financials customers in October twenty-twenty-six. Anaplan's Agentic Enterprise deploys skills-based agents covering FP&A, treasury, controllership, and procurement on Amazon Bedrock.
Datarails, in twenty-twenty-six, introduced AI finance agents for strategy, planning, and reporting; in March twenty-twenty-six it also launched FinanceOS, described as a governed foundation connecting financial data, business logic, workflows, applications, and AI across the office of the CFO.
**The BCG Deployment Benchmark:** BCG data show that as much as eighty percent of FP&A work is still spent extracting and packaging data and performing simple calculations; agentic AI will move finance teams from producing reports to interpreting performance and advising the business. In one documented deployment, a finance insight agent automated more than ninety percent of business intelligence work in nine months -- work that previously took three years.
**CFO Budget Signal:** Fifty-four percent of CFOs are planning agentic deployments as a twenty-twenty-six transformation priority, specifically systems that autonomously trigger reforecasts, process payments within policy, and surface risk signals without human initiation. CFOs now allocate about a quarter of their AI budgets specifically to agentic projects.
**The OCC Governance Consequence:** The new OCC supervisory framework means that every agentic FP&A pilot inside a bank, regardless of whether it was purchased as a product feature inside Workday, Anaplan, or a point solution, now needs to be inventoried and defensible under examination. This is a demand accelerator for governance tooling and a brake on undocumented pilots. Banks buying agentic FP&A tools in Q4 and into twenty-twenty-seven should expect procurement conversations to include audit trails, model risk documentation under SR 26-2, and human override design as standard contract requirements.
---
### CFO Agenda, FP&A, and Transformation Signals
**The CPI Data Gap as a Planning Forcing Function:** A CFO cannot model a year-over-year inflation trajectory from tomorrow's release. The practical consequence is that December hike scenario planning must run on month-over-month velocity and Fed speaker signals rather than the annual CPI anchor that typically feeds budget rate assumptions. Deutsche Bank notes the market pivots this week from payrolls toward October CPI and PPI, with PPI due Friday as well. Natixis chief US economist Christopher Hodge writes that with inflation sticky above target and the labor market stable, another hike will be warranted in December.
**Finance Transformation Demand Forces Active This Week:**
- Regulatory rebuild: Basel finalization pending, SR 26-2 live, OCC AI framework published -- all three create concurrent documentation and system requirements that manual finance teams cannot absorb. - Cost-versus-workload squeeze: eighty percent of FP&A effort is still data packaging, and a December hike would add a third rate-scenario planning cycle in four months. - AI maturation and buying patterns: the evidence is that agentic finance is moving from pilot to procurement, with CFOs concentrating roughly a quarter of AI spend on agentic projects. Banks at earlier stages are now entering a catch-up window. - Deposit and funding economics: the wholesale-to-core deposit rotation visible across reported banks signals a treasury workload surge in Q4 -- hedge restructuring, FHLB repayment modeling, and CD rollover analysis -- all candidates for automation.
---
### Contrarian Insight
The consensus framing treats the CPI data gap as a nuisance. The more useful framing for a bank CFO is that it is a hidden planning gift. Because the BLS cannot publish an annual rate tomorrow, the December FOMC decision will be forced to weight real-time labor and activity data more heavily relative to the inflation print than in any prior cycle. That shifts the risk weighting back toward the jobs market -- where October's one hundred sixty-five thousand print was already the dominant upside surprise. Banks that have been anchoring December hike scenarios to a presumed CPI softening should revisit: the absence of an annual CPI number does not reduce the probability of a hike; it removes one of the few data points that could have argued against it.
---
### Client Conversation Hooks
1. **The CPI data gap question:** "Your CFO's December hike assumption is probably built on a CPI trajectory. Tomorrow's report will not publish a year-over-year rate because of the twenty-twenty-five government shutdown. How is your planning team adjusting its December scenario weights when the inflation anchor goes dark?"
2. **The OCC agentic AI examination posture:** "The OCC just published its first supervisory framework for agentic AI in bank operations. If your finance team has any AI agents running in FP&A, close, or treasury -- even as a vendor-embedded feature -- those are now examinable. Do you have an agent inventory and human override design ready for an examiner conversation?"
3. **The wholesale funding paydown playbook:** "First Horizon and Mercantile are both using non-core asset sales and organic deposit growth to systematically pay down brokered and FHLB funding before year-end. Is your treasury function running a similar optimization, and does your finance system give you the scenario modeling to know what a dollar of wholesale paydown is worth to NIM under a December hike versus a hold?"

item.title: Finance Pulse - Nov 6, 2026
item.description:
I'll run all major searches simultaneously across macro, rates, banking, regulatory, and AI-in-finance domains to capture the freshest developments as of November 6, 2026.Now let me run one final search to capture the most current November 6 news on the October jobs report and any breaking bank or regulatory developments.I now have comprehensive, fresh data across all required domains. Here are the genuinely new angles for November 6, 2026, not covered in prior episodes:
1. **The October payrolls print is the live macro event of the day**: consensus is 59,000 to 65,000 jobs added, wage growth expected to slow to 2.9% year-on-year, potentially the first sub-3% reading in five and a half years. December hike odds collapsed from 82.7% to roughly 69% overnight on the equity rout. This is a qualitatively new rate-path signal. 2. **A sharp equity selloff is reshaping the December hike calculus in real time**: the Nasdaq 100 fell 6.36% Thursday, its worst single-day drop since March 2020. The 10-year Treasury is at 4.82% to 4.84% and the 2s10s spread has widened to 38 basis points, a structurally important curve shape for bank NIM planning. 3. **PNC disclosed a CFO transition**: Robert Q. Reilly exits to Executive Vice Chairman on March 1, 2027, with Alexander Overstrom taking the seat, triggering a 4.2% after-hours slide and shedding $3.6 billion in market value. 4. **Basel III Endgame still pending**: as of late September 2026, the final rule is not yet issued. The comment period closed June 18, 2026. KPMG analysis flags potential net capital relief and capital redeployment opportunities for super-regionals. 5. **Super-regional AI moves are concrete and Q3-verified**: KeyCorp CFO specifically cited AI automating high-volume consumer-servicing tasks and streamlining commercial originations. Fifth Third's CEO committed to sustained AI investment post-Comerica conversion. 6. **The governance gap in AI is the critical new angle**: Gartner data shows 60% of finance teams are piloting or implementing AI, but only 7% of CFOs say those investments are having a strong impact, a signal that separates real deployments from vendor marketing. 7. **The 2s10s curve widening to 38 basis points is a new NIM planning wedge**: combined with softening wage growth, this curve geometry is distinct from prior episodes.
---
## Finance Pulse | Friday, November 6, 2026
**Bottom line: October payrolls data arriving this morning into the most fragile equity backdrop of the year is simultaneously repricing the December hike probability downward and widening the 2s10s curve to 38 basis points, a geometry that reshapes every bank CFO's Q4 NIM assumption, while PNC's CFO transition and the persistent governance gap in AI deployments both signal that the finance transformation demand cycle is rotating from sell-side enthusiasm to prove-it accountability.**
---
### Top Takeaways
1. The two-year Treasury yield fell 12 basis points to 4.46% and the ten-year dropped to 4.84%, widening the 2s10s spread to 38 basis points, while CME FedWatch priced a 68.6% probability of a December hike on November 5, down sharply from 82.7% the prior day. 2. PNC's CFO Robert Q. Reilly will shift to Executive Vice Chairman on March 1, 2027, with Alexander Overstrom taking the finance seat, an event that unsettles investors who prize continuity at a large regional bank where the finance chief's read on credit and capital allocation carries significant weight. 3. By 2026, Gartner predicts 90% of finance functions will deploy at least one AI-enabled technology solution, yet close to 60% of finance teams are piloting or implementing AI projects while only 7% of CFOs say those investments are having a strong impact.
---
### Key Themes
**Theme 1 (New): The payrolls-curve-rates triangle is repricing December in real time.** US nonfarm payrolls are expected to have risen modestly in October, with annual wage growth anticipated to slow to below 3.0% for the first time in nearly five and a half years, reinforcing the view that the labor market is not a source of inflation. Average hourly earnings are forecast to have increased 0.3% in October. Bond traders are positioned for further Treasury gains as expectations for additional Fed rate hikes fade, with a global stock selloff following the midterm elections driving investors to bonds and taking yields to their lowest since early September.
**Theme 2 (Evolving): The Basel III Endgame finalization clock is still running but the opportunity framing has shifted.** The original 2023 proposal was effectively scrapped and replaced with something far less aggressive; Category III and IV banks can now choose whether to adopt the Expanded Risk-Based Approach or continue under a revised Standardized Approach, giving mid-sized regional banks more flexibility than the largest GSIBs. KPMG's regulatory analysis flags a potential for net capital relief under the revised framework, with recalibration creating opportunities for banks to reassess binding constraints, release excess management buffers, and redeploy capital toward lending growth, balance sheet optimization, and M&A.
**Theme 3 (New): The AI governance gap is now the CFO's accountability problem.** Boards have shifted from asking what AI can do to asking what it can return, and CFOs now have to fund the transformation, prove value early, and reinvent finance at the same time. Deloitte's Q4 2025 CFO Signals survey found that 54% of CFOs say integrating AI agents into their finance departments will be a top transformation priority in 2026, and 87% believe AI will be very important to finance operations this year.
---
### Banking Finance-Function
**NIM and curve geometry:** The 2s10s widening to 38 basis points is the most important structural change in the rates picture since the September hike. A wider curve benefits banks that hold longer-duration assets funded with shorter-term deposits, but the benefit is asymmetric: banks that locked in wholesale funding at higher rates face persistent cost drag while asset yields begin repricing higher.
**PNC leadership signal:** The CFO transition timeline stretches to March 2027, giving PNC time to manage the handoff, but markets rarely wait for the calendar to catch up with a headline, and the stock shed $3.6 billion in market value on the news. For a finance transformation consultant, this is a classic buying-window signal: incoming CFOs at institutions of PNC's scale typically accelerate vendor reviews and operating-model assessments within their first 90 days.
**Super-regional AI in core operations:** Third-quarter results from PNC, U.S. Bancorp, Truist, Fifth Third, Regions, and KeyCorp show regional banks putting AI into everyday banking operations; KeyCorp CFO Clark Khayat said Key is using AI to automate high-volume consumer-servicing tasks and streamline credit and collateral processes in commercial originations. Fifth Third also identified AI as an internal investment priority, with CEO Tim Spence committing to sustain long-term investment in growth and AI following the Comerica conversion.
**Wage growth deceleration and headcount math:** If October wages print below 3% year-on-year, it confirms that labor cost inflation for banks is finally easing. This is directly relevant to efficiency ratio planning and the cost-side of the finance function's own operating model.
---
### Regulatory Radar
The Basel III Endgame comment period closed on June 18, 2026, and as of September 19 the March 2026 proposals remain pending a final rule. Two related rules did finalize: the enhanced supplementary leverage ratio in November 2025 and community bank leverage ratio changes in April 2026.
The choice given to Category III and IV banks between the Expanded Risk-Based Approach and a revised Standardized Approach reflects a broader recalibration in US regulatory policy, driven by industry lobbying over the original proposal's cost, competitiveness concerns relative to international peers, and a change in political and regulatory leadership.
For finance function leaders: the pending final rule means capital planning models must simultaneously hold two scenario sets, one under the ERBA and one under the revised Standardized Approach, a modeling workload that is driving demand for scenario-capable FP&A platforms.
---
### AI in Finance
**The governance gap is the signal:** Roughly 60% of finance teams are piloting or implementing AI projects, while only 7% of CFOs say those investments are having a strong impact, with the gap stemming from architectural limitations. This is the clearest differentiation point between banks that are genuinely transforming and those accumulating pilots.
**Where real deployments live:** OneStream has announced the general availability of its Finance Agentic Layer, allowing CFO offices to deploy AI agents that interact directly with financial data models. SAP's agentic AI rollout spans FP&A, tax, and treasury, as the company moves to an end-to-end approach for automating finance workflows. These are vendor-announced capabilities, not independently verified bank deployments, but they signal where the platform spend is concentrating.
**The buy-side pattern:** Organizations report finance teams using agentic FP&A tools can spend 70% of their time on analysis rather than data preparation; HPE's finance team is deploying agentic AI in treasury following successful AP and AR pilots, a sequencing pattern reflecting the logical expansion path as organizational confidence grows. The AP-to-treasury sequencing is the architecture a bank finance team should map to its own function.
**BCG's accountability framing:** Today, as much as 80% of FP&A work is still spent extracting and packaging data and performing simple calculations; agentic AI will move finance teams from producing reports to interpreting performance and advising the business.
---
### CFO Agenda, FP&A, and Transformation Signals
Three forces are creating demand for finance change right now:
1. **Rate-path uncertainty compressing the planning window.** With December hike probability dropping from 83% to 69% overnight, CFOs cannot anchor annual plans to a single rate scenario. This is a direct driver of demand for scenario-capable budgeting and forecasting platforms.
2. **CFO transition at PNC as a buying signal.** Incoming CFOs at institutions of PNC's scale typically accelerate vendor reviews. Alexander Overstrom takes the seat in March 2027, meaning vendor engagement conversations at PNC will heat up through Q1.
3. **The 7% impact problem is the ROI conversation clients need to have.** Boards have moved quickly from asking what AI can do to asking what it can return, and CFOs now have to fund the transformation, prove value early, and reinvent finance at the same time. Finance transformation consultants who can build a credible ROI framework around deployed agents, not pilots, will win the mandate.
---
### Contrarian Insight
The curve-widening narrative is being read as uniformly positive for bank NIM. It is not. Banks that aggressively repriced deposits upward during the flat-curve period to retain balances now face a stickier cost of funds even as the front end softens. The 2s10s widening benefits the asset side, but liability repricing lags. The CFOs who win Q4 and 2027 planning season are those who built deposit-mix analytics granular enough to model the lag separately from the asset-side benefit, not those who applied a blended beta assumption.
---
### Client Conversation Hooks
1. **The 7% impact question.** When you meet with a bank finance leader who says "we have AI pilots running," ask how many of them have crossed from pilot to production workflow, and what the CFO is reporting to the board on ROI. That 7% strong-impact figure is your opening.
2. **The PNC CFO transition opportunity.** New finance chiefs at super-regionals reset vendor relationships. The transition timeline runs to March 2027. Who is in front of the incoming CFO at PNC right now?
3. **The dual-scenario capital modeling burden.** With the Basel III Endgame final rule still pending and Category III and IV banks holding optionality between the ERBA and the revised Standardized Approach, ask your super-regional clients how many FTEs are manually maintaining parallel capital scenario models, and whether that workload has shown up in their technology budget conversations yet.

item.title: Finance Pulse - Nov 5, 2026
item.description:
I'll run all major searches simultaneously across macro, rates, banking, regulatory, and AI-in-finance domains to capture the freshest developments as of November 5, 2026.Now let me run one final targeted search to capture the freshest November 5 news on treasury yield moves, employment data, and any breaking bank finance news.I now have strong, fresh sourced material across all required domains. Here are the genuinely new angles for November 5, 2026, not covered in prior episodes:
1. **The midterm election result is the dominant macro catalyst today**: Democrats swept Congress on November 4, sending Treasury yields lower and equities sharply higher. The 10-year yield, which touched a session high of 4.97% on JOLTS strength Tuesday, has pulled back to near 4.92% after the Democratic win, introducing a new fiscal-gridlock scenario that is distinct from prior episodes' rate-path focus.
2. **The October nonfarm payrolls report drops today (Friday, November 7) and is the market's next pivot point**: ADP came in at 86,000 private-sector jobs in October, with consensus for NFP at 65,000. JOLTS showed 7.52 million openings for September. This labor-market data trio is new and directly shapes the December 9 rate call.
3. **The Cleveland Fed's November 3 nowcast puts October PCE at 3.77% headline and core PCE at 3.20%**, ahead of the November 25 BEA release -- a new and actionable planning figure not in prior episodes.
4. **The CME FedWatch tool, as of November 5, puts December hike probability at 80.2%**, up from 76.2% a week ago and from the 77% OIS-implied figure covered in the November 4 recap -- the direction of travel is hardening, and the specific tool-by-tool divergence (CME at 80.2% versus OIS at 77%) is a new analytical wedge.
5. **BNY Markets' John Velis explicitly frames the 2027 path as "much murkier"** even while confirming December, a named-firm call that introduces the post-December uncertainty angle as a CFO planning problem.
6. **The Basel III Endgame final rule remains pending with no effective date set**, comment period closed June 18, 2026. The KPMG framing of potential net capital relief for super-regionals (Category III/IV getting a choice of ERBA or revised Standardized Approach) is a fresh CFO planning positive not previously framed from the demand-release perspective.
7. **OneStream's Finance Agentic Layer is now generally available** -- a named, specific product launch with direct banking CFO relevance, distinct from the BCG/vendor-trend framing used in prior episodes.
8. **BCG's Agentic Leadership Playbook surfaces the 80% / 20% inversion**: today as much as 80% of FP&A work is data extraction and packaging; agentic AI is the mechanism to flip that ratio. The playbook also surfaces the board-level ROI accountability shift -- boards asking "what does AI return?" -- as a new governance pressure on bank CFOs.
9. **Political gridlock scenario and its effect on the yield curve** -- Democratic Congress versus Trump White House now sets up a fiscal tug-of-war that could structurally suppress long-end yields even with a December hike, a new angle for bank ALCO and treasury planning.
---
## Finance Pulse | Thursday, November 5, 2026
**Bottom line: The Democrats' midterm sweep has introduced a fiscal gridlock scenario that is pulling long-end yields off their highs even as the December hike probability hardened overnight to eighty point two percent on CME FedWatch -- creating a rare planning moment where the short end rises but the long end is capped, compressing the yield curve in a direction that challenges NIM assumptions built on steepening. Meanwhile, the Cleveland Fed's November third nowcast puts October core PCE at three point two percent, ahead of the November twenty-fifth BEA release, keeping the inflation pressure alive. And OneStream's Finance Agentic Layer reaching general availability marks the clearest signal yet that agentic AI has crossed from pilot to procurement decision.**
---
### Top Takeaways
1. **Midterm politics have become a rates variable.** Treasury yields fell after Democrats swept Congress, introducing a fiscal-gridlock dynamic that could structurally cap 10-year yields -- a new ALCO planning input that did not exist 48 hours ago. 2. **The December hike is nearly priced in, but the 2027 path is wide open.** CME FedWatch sits at 80.2% for a December 9 hike; BNY Markets explicitly labels 2027 as "much murkier," making the multi-year planning horizon the real CFO challenge. 3. **OneStream's agentic finance layer is live.** The general availability of OneStream's Finance Agentic Layer converts a vendor roadmap item into an active procurement decision for bank CFOs evaluating their EPM stack. 4. **NFP today is the swing factor for December.** ADP showed 86,000 October jobs; consensus for nonfarm payrolls is 65,000. A strong print re-steepens the front end and gives the Fed cover; a miss opens the door to a December hold. 5. **Super-regional NIM tailwind is real but bifurcated by deposit-cost discipline.** Q3 data across the community and regional cohort shows NIMs expanding where deposit costs are controlled (e.g., First Bank, deposit cost rising only 5 basis points to 2.47%), and lagging where they are not.
---
### Key Themes
**Theme 1 (New): The Fiscal Gridlock Yield-Curve Compression Trade** Democrats holding Congress against a Trump White House creates a legislative stalemate on spending. The 10-year Treasury yield stood near 4.92% on November 4, having pulled back sharply after the election results. Treasury yields fell as investors sought shelter, sparked by Democratic election victories. Election-related uncertainty is now off the table after President Trump said he'd recognize the results and vowed to work with Democrats. For bank ALCOs, the implication is a constrained long end even as the short end gets one more push from a December hike -- a flatter or mildly inverted curve that pressures NIM assumptions built on a steepening scenario.
**Theme 2 (Evolving): December Hike Nearly Certain, But 2027 Is the Real Planning Gap** The CME FedWatch Tool, updated November 5, shows an 80.2% probability of a hike to the 4.00 to 4.25 percent range at the December 9 meeting, up from 76.2% the previous week. J.P. Morgan's chief U.S. economist Michael Feroli reads the October statement as a hawkish bias that keeps December live, stating: "We continue to expect a hike at the December FOMC meeting." The bank does not see December opening a longer series of increases. More importantly for multi-year budgeting, BNY Markets' John Velis maintains the view of one additional hike in December to preserve Fed credibility, but notes the landscape heading into 2027 "appears much murkier." The December meeting also brings a new dot plot -- the first since September -- which will be the primary planning document for 2027 bank budgets.
**Theme 3 (New): NFP as Today's Swing Factor** ADP reported that private companies added 86,000 jobs in October, slightly ahead of the Dow Jones estimate for 75,000. Consensus for nonfarm payrolls is 65,000. September JOLTS showed 7.523 million job openings, beating the 7.125 million economist consensus. A payrolls print materially above consensus reinforces the December hike and pressures the front end further; a miss introduces genuine hold risk that bank treasury desks have not fully priced. The October CPI release follows on November 10, with the Cleveland Fed nowcast as of November 3 putting October CPI at 3.74% year-over-year and core PCE at 3.20%.
---
### Banking Finance-Function Metrics
**NIM and Deposit Costs -- The Discipline Gap Widens** Q3 earnings data confirms that deposit-cost discipline, not rate exposure alone, is what separates NIM winners. First Bank's net interest margin expanded six basis points sequentially to 3.74% on a tax-equivalent basis, while deposit costs rose at a slower pace, increasing just five basis points to 2.47%. BankUnited's net interest margin reached 3.16%, up 16 basis points year over year, as average deposit costs fell 39 basis points. The contrasting story: Bank of Hawai'i's deposit repricing and mix shifts had a negative 1.4 million dollar quarterly impact on net interest income, with rate-sensitive earning assets projected to add an estimated 4.1 million dollars to quarterly net interest income while deposit costs would reduce it by 3.1 million in the short term.
**Credit and Provisioning** Higher credit costs are appearing at the margin. Shore Bancshares delivered strong NIM expansion to 3.78% but reported margin excluding accretion of only 3.50%, a 28-basis-point gap that reveals accretion dependence as a risk in the provisioning outlook. This accretion reliance is an underexplored vulnerability in super-regional credit cost planning.
**Inflation's direct balance-sheet effect** US PCE inflation accelerated to 3.6% year-on-year in September 2026 from 3.4% in August, while core PCE picked up to 3.1% from 3.0%. US real disposable income fell 0.3% as PCE inflation hit 3.6%. Compressed real income directly feeds consumer delinquency risk in bank loan books -- a credit provisioning input that connects inflation data to expected loss modeling.
---
### Regulatory Radar
**Basel III Endgame -- Awaiting Final Rule, With a Capital Release Optionality Angle** As of September 19, 2026, the March 2026 proposals remain pending a final rule. Category III and IV banks can choose whether to adopt the Expanded Risk-Based Approach or continue under a revised Standardized Approach, giving mid-sized regional banks more flexibility than the largest GSIBs. The underexplored CFO angle: KPMG's regulatory analysis notes potential for net capital relief, with recalibration creating opportunities for banks to reassess binding constraints, release excess management buffers, and redeploy capital toward lending growth, balance sheet optimization, and M&A. For super-regional finance teams, the question is no longer "how do we absorb the capital hit?" but "how do we model the capital optionality?" -- a demand signal for scenario-modeling and capital planning technology upgrades.
**December Dot Plot as Regulatory Corollary** The December 9 SEP and dot plot carry direct regulatory planning weight. The December 2026 meeting is one of four that include the Summary of Economic Projections. Whatever the median 2027 rate projection signals will drive DFAST scenario calibration, ALCO stress-test assumptions, and the liquidity coverage ratio planning that bank treasurers must lock in for Q1 2027.
---
### AI in Finance
**OneStream's Finance Agentic Layer -- From Roadmap to Live Procurement Decision** OneStream recently announced the general availability of its Finance Agentic Layer, allowing CFO offices to deploy AI agents that interact directly with financial data models. This is the clearest signal in the EPM market that agentic AI has crossed from vendor marketing to an active buying decision. For bank CFOs evaluating OneStream versus legacy Oracle Hyperion or SAP BPC migrations, this release changes the competitive calculus: the platform question is now inseparable from the AI-agent strategy question.
**The 80/20 Inversion Is Now the BCG Planning Framework** BCG finds that as much as 80% of FP&A work is still spent extracting and packaging data and performing simple calculations, and that agentic AI will move finance teams from producing reports to interpreting performance and advising the business. Boards have shifted from asking what AI can do to asking what it can return, leaving CFOs to fund the transformation, prove value early, and reinvent finance at the same time. For bank CFOs, this is a governance pressure, not just a technology one: the board is now asking for an ROI narrative on the AI investment, not just a pilot update.
**SAP and the CFO's Expanding System Mandate** SAP rolled out a broad new set of agentic AI tools for CFOs in May 2026, as competition intensified among enterprise software vendors racing to embed the technology across finance operations. The AI shift is pushing CFOs beyond traditional finance responsibilities into enterprise system strategy, with SAP's CFO product leader noting that "the CFO is starting to also really have a role and responsibility for those decisions." For bank finance transformation leaders, this is the architecture conversation: the CFO function is now a system-of-record decision-maker, not just a data consumer.
**AI Governance Emerging as a Board-Level Priority** Three AI FP&A trends are most consequential in 2026: the shift to continuous planning powered by self-updating ML models; agentic AI moving from pilot to production; and AI governance for financial outputs emerging as a board-level priority, driven by EY's September 2026 AI Risk and Governance Survey findings on the confidence gap. For regulated banks, AI governance in finance carries a direct model-risk management overlay -- a demand signal for model validation frameworks applied to AI-generated forecasts and regulatory reports.
---
### CFO Agenda, FP&A, and Transformation Signals
**The Planning Assumption That Changed Overnight** Every bank CFO who built a 2027 budget on a steepening yield curve now has to revisit the long-end assumption after the Democratic sweep. The gridlock scenario constrains fiscal expansion and historically correlates with anchored long-end yields. This is not a technical adjustment; it is a full NII sensitivity re-run.
**The Deposit Cost Discipline Imperative** Q3 data makes clear that the variance in NIM performance within the peer group is primarily explained by deposit repricing speed and mix management, not asset yields. This is the finance transformation demand signal for real-time deposit analytics and behavioral modeling -- the bank equivalent of the customer analytics investment that retail companies made a decade ago.
**Capital Optionality Under the Revised Basel Framework** Super-regional CFOs should be building scenario models for the ERBA adoption decision rather than simply waiting for the final rule. The flexibility embedded in the March 2026 proposals for Category III and IV banks means that the capital planning function needs to run parallel-path analysis now, before finalization.
**Agentic AI Governance as the New Model Risk Management Frontier** As agentic AI moves into production in FP&A, controllership, and regulatory reporting, bank model risk management frameworks have not yet caught up. The EY confidence gap finding is the market signal that this governance infrastructure -- AI model validation, audit trail standards, explainability requirements for regulatory submissions -- is the next wave of transformation investment at large banks.
---
### Contrarian Insight
**The conventional wisdom is that NIM expansion is the tailwind story of 2026 for banks. The contrarian read from Q3 data is that accretion income is doing more work than the headlines suggest.** Shore Bancshares' reported NIM of 3.78% collapses to 3.50% excluding accretion -- a 28-basis-point gap. If this pattern holds across the super-regional cohort, the NIM recovery story is partly a one-time asset-repricing artifact, not a durable funding-structure improvement. When accretion rolls off in 2027, the NIMs that look strongest today may reveal the softest underlying deposit-cost structures. CFOs building multi-year NII forecasts should be isolating accretion contribution as a separate line item in their sensitivity models, not burying it in the blended margin.
---
### Client Conversation Hooks
1. **"The Democratic sweep just changed your ALCO assumption."** The gridlock scenario structurally caps the long end even as the short end gets another hike. Has your bank re-run its NII sensitivity under a flat-to-inverted curve that holds for 18 months rather than steepening into 2027?
2. **"OneStream's Finance Agentic Layer is now generally available. Is your EPM platform decision also an AI-agent strategy decision?"** For any bank still running Oracle Hyperion or evaluating SAP BPC, the platform RFP is no longer a pure technology question -- it is an agentic workflow question that the CFO now owns alongside IT.
3. **"How much of your NIM expansion is accretion, and what happens when it rolls off?"** The Shore Bancshares example illustrates a 28-basis-point gap between reported and ex-accretion NIM. Super-regional CFOs who cannot answer this question cleanly are carrying a hidden planning risk into 2027 budget season.

item.title: Finance Pulse - Nov 4, 2026
item.description:
I now have comprehensive fresh data across all required domains. Let me compile both outputs.
---
## Finance Pulse | Wednesday, November 4, 2026
**Bottom line: The Fed's October hold at three point seven five to four percent has dramatically reshuffled the December hike calculus, with OIS markets now pricing a seventy-seven percent probability of a December ninth move, energy-driven headline inflation entrenching itself at three point seven percent while Bloomberg's trimmed-mean measure sits at two point two percent, and Q3 super-regional earnings revealing a bifurcated NIM story where balance-sheet discipline separates winners from laggards. The finance transformation demand signal is now unambiguous: BCG data show agentic FP&A deployments compressing three-year transformations into nine months, and the Basel III Endgame finalization clock is ticking toward a Q4 2026 rule that delivers net capital relief rather than the burden CFOs once feared.**
---
### Top Takeaways
1. The Fed held on October twenty-eighth but two governors dissented in favor of a hike, and OIS pricing has since moved to a seventy-seven percent implied probability of a December ninth increase, making December the definitive planning fulcrum for bank CFOs. 2. Bloomberg's independent Price Project puts trimmed-mean inflation at two point two percent through October, materially below the official three point seven percent CPI print, suggesting energy distortion is masking genuine disinflation in the core basket. 3. PNC's Q3 NIM compressed two basis points sequentially to two point nine four percent even as NII grew fifteen percent year-over-year, illustrating how deposit-cost creep is now offsetting asset repricing gains for large commercial banks. 4. KeyCorp delivered record revenue above two billion dollars in Q3 with a cash efficiency ratio of sixty point six percent, reaffirming its three point two five percent-plus NIM target for late 2027 as a forward planning benchmark for the cohort. 5. BCG's agentic leadership playbook documents a real deployment where finance insight agents automated more than ninety percent of FP&A business-intelligence work in nine months, compressing what previously took three years. 6. The Basel III Endgame final rule is expected in Q4 2026, with implementation beginning in 2027, delivering an estimated eighty-seven point seven billion dollars in net capital relief for the industry rather than the originally proposed nineteen percent increase.
---
### Key Themes
**Theme 1 (New): The October Hold Dissent and What It Signals for December Planning** The Fed voted ten to two at its late October meeting to hold rates steady at three point seventy-five to four percent, with Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissenting in favor of a quarter-point increase. The next FOMC decision is on December ninth, and as of November third, OIS pricing implies a seventy-seven percent chance of a twenty-five basis-point hike at that meeting. Over the next twelve months, markets price a net fifty-eight point four basis points of hikes, or approximately two point three hikes at a twenty-five basis-point step. For CFOs, the planning implication is concrete: a December hike would push funding costs higher into year-end exactly as annual budgets are being finalized, compressing the deposit-cost assumptions embedded in 2027 NII forecasts.
**Theme 2 (Evolving): Inflation's Split Personality and the CFO's Forecasting Dilemma** The BLS reported on October fourteenth that US CPI rose zero point six percent in September and three point seven percent over twelve months, with core at two point six percent. The PPI release of October fifteenth printed six point three percent, the largest twelve-month increase since December 2022. Yet Bloomberg's alternative read is significantly more sanguine: Bloomberg's trimmed-mean shows the underlying pace of inflation at two point two percent through October, already close to the Fed's two percent target and below the two point seven percent reported by the Cleveland Fed. In aggregate, Bloomberg's data confirms that inflation is too high and the Iran conflict is the main reason, with motor fuel up thirty-nine point nine percent from a year earlier. The divergence between headline CPI and trimmed-mean is the operative CFO forecasting problem: which gauge drives the Fed, and which one models deposit-pricing competition more accurately?
**Theme 3 (New): The Basel III Endgame Finalization Countdown Is Now Real** Regulators spent 2023 designing a rule to make the largest US banks hold roughly nineteen percent more capital. In March 2026, the same three agencies published a re-proposal delivering the opposite outcome: an estimated eighty-seven point seven billion dollars in net capital relief for the industry. The public comment period closed on June eighteenth, and finalization is targeted for Q4 2026, with implementation beginning in 2027. Although the 2026 Endgame proposal would increase required capital in some dimensions, when taken together with the various capital rules proposed and finalized since 2025, the net impact would decrease required capital. For finance transformation, the finalization event creates a mandatory regulatory reporting rebuild, a capital-planning model refresh, and stress-testing recalibration across all Category I through IV institutions.
---
### Banking Finance-Function Metrics
**PNC Q3 2026:** PNC reported solid Q3 2026 performance, characterized by fifteen percent year-over-year NII growth to four point two billion dollars and fourteen percent year-over-year loan growth to three hundred seventy-nine billion dollars. However, NIM compressed two basis points sequentially to two point nine four percent as deposit costs rose modestly. Total rate paid on interest-bearing deposits increased seven basis points to one point nine eight percent, including brokered CDs. PNC remains on track to reach its goal of reducing costs by three hundred fifty million dollars in 2026 through its continuous improvement program, which is independent of the FirstBank acquisition.
**KeyCorp Q3 2026:** KeyCorp presented Q3 2026 earnings on October twentieth, beating profit expectations with earnings of zero point five one dollars per share, up twenty-four percent year-over-year, while delivering record revenue of two point zero four billion dollars. The cash efficiency ratio improved to sixty point six percent, down one hundred fifty-four basis points year-over-year on an adjusted basis. Total deposit costs increased three basis points to one point six six percent, with management indicating deposit beta should continue moving higher as the competitive deposit environment persists. KeyCorp expanded NIM to two point nine five percent and reaffirmed its three point two five percent-plus NIM target for late 2027.
**Truist:** Fee income is doing the heavy lifting at Truist, with noninterest income up twelve percent year-over-year to one point five five billion dollars, investment banking and trading up thirty-six point three percent, and deposit costs falling twenty-four basis points year-over-year to one point five five percent.
**Deposit-Cost Bifurcation Signal:** Mercantile Bank offers a sharp contrast to peers. Mercantile successfully optimized its funding base, reducing high-cost brokered deposits from four hundred fifty-seven million dollars at year-end 2025 to just twenty million dollars as of September 2026. This shift, combined with eleven point four percent annualized growth in local deposits, fueled a twenty-four basis-point year-over-year NIM expansion to three point seven three percent. This is a decisive illustration for CFOs: the gap between banks that actively managed their deposit mix versus those that allowed brokered-funding dependence to persist is now measurable in NIM.
---
### Regulatory Radar
The Basel III Endgame finalization is the dominant regulatory event of Q4 2026. A primary change in the 2026 re-proposal is the removal of the dual-stack framework, where banks calculated capital ratios under both standardized and internal models. The updated proposal emphasizes a simpler structure to reduce complexity and improve transparency, with regulators signaling a clear preference for standardized methodologies for credit and operational risk, replacing bank-specific models with a common language that enhances comparability and provides long-term capital predictability.
The regime shift from internal models to standardized approaches has a direct finance-function consequence that is under-discussed: it makes the capital-reporting process more comparable across institutions but requires a wholesale rebuild of the data pipelines and calculation engines that currently feed regulatory reports. The 2026 Endgame proposal would also decrease the amount of capital held by the depository subsidiaries of Category I and II banks, which means those banks could shift capital from the subsidiary to the holding company, a structural change requiring treasury and capital-planning teams to rebuild their inter-entity allocation models.
The FOMC's internal division is itself a regulatory radar item: Warsh was not willing to call current financial conditions tight, potentially signaling room for additional rate hikes, and in a sign the Fed remains divided, he described the latest meeting as a serious, sober discussion.
---
### AI in Finance
The clearest new signal this week is BCG's agentic leadership playbook, which names the CFO's finance transformation problem precisely. In one deployment, a finance insight agent automated more than ninety percent of the work in nine months, compressing a transformation that had previously taken three years. Today, as much as eighty percent of FP&A work is still spent extracting and packaging data and performing simple calculations. For banks specifically, BCG notes that better insight into deposit stickiness can change how much liquidity buffer they need to hold, connecting the FP&A use case directly to treasury and ALM planning.
As of Q3 2026, finance teams are navigating a fragmented landscape of AI-enhanced tools. SAP's recent push, highlighted in CFO Dive's August 2026 coverage, emphasizes embedding AI agents directly into S/4HANA Finance modules to reduce context-switching. However, integration complexity and data silos continue to hinder widespread deployment, which is the most honest sentence in vendor-landscape coverage this cycle.
On ROI credibility and what banks are actually buying: financial institutions are deploying AI at speed but measuring returns inconsistently. The institutions generating the highest measurable ROI share three traits: centralized AI infrastructure rather than project-by-project build, model risk management frameworks embedded from the start, and CFO-defined output metrics set before go-live, not after.
The first fully agentic M&A due diligence systems, processing fifty thousand to one hundred thousand documents with minimal human review, are already in deployment at two tier-one banks. By 2027, agentic due diligence is projected to compress deal timelines by forty percent and eliminate a full layer of junior analyst work from the deal pipeline. For finance transformation consultants, this is the signal that banks are not waiting for universal platform readiness; they are deploying point-solution agentic systems in high-value, high-document workflows first.
Organizations using agentic FP&A tools report finance teams spending seventy percent of their time on analysis and decision support rather than data preparation. HPE's finance team is deploying agentic AI in treasury functions following successful AP and AR pilots, a sequencing pattern that mirrors the logical expansion path banks are following.
**Governance and the buy-versus-build divide:** CFOs now allocate approximately twenty-five percent of AI budgets to agentic AI initiatives, reflecting significant confidence in the category. But the governance gap remains the barrier: the shift in 2026 is from copilot suggestions to agents that execute workflows under governance. An AI copilot suggests or drafts; a human reviews every output. Banks moving to execution-layer agents without model risk governance infrastructure are accumulating technical debt that regulators will eventually price.
---
### CFO Agenda, FP&A, and Transformation Signals
Three forces are creating acute demand for finance transformation at banks right now, and they are distinct from what prior episodes have surfaced:
**1. The December hike as a budget deadline:** A December ninth hike would land as 2027 budgets are being signed off. CFOs who built NIM assumptions on a stable rate environment face a mid-budget-cycle adjustment. The demand signal is for scenario-planning infrastructure that can re-run NII sensitivity in hours, not weeks.
**2. The capital-relief windfall requires new allocation models:** For Category I and II banks, the Basel III Endgame re-proposal is projected to require banks to hold one point six percent more capital, which is far less than feared, but the freed capital must be reallocated. Treasury teams without dynamic capital-allocation tools will manually model subsidiary-to-holding-company capital movement at a time when precision is highest-stakes.
**3. M&A integration is raising the finance workload bar:** PNC's FirstBank integration is running concurrently with its three hundred fifty million dollar cost-reduction program. Results reflected higher NII, solid loan and deposit growth, and improved operating efficiency, but higher expenses and increased net loan charge-offs were headwinds. The finance function at acquiring banks is being asked to do more with the same headcount during integration: a classic workload-versus-budget squeeze that accelerates demand for automation.
---
### Contrarian Insight
The consensus framing is that higher-for-longer rates are uniformly bad for bank funding costs and therefore for NIM. But the Q3 earnings data tells a more nuanced story: banks that had already done the hard work of exiting brokered deposits and rebuilding relationship-funded balance sheets are expanding NIM in this environment. After removing the impact of purchase accounting, Bank First showed each sequential quarter of 2026 exhibiting higher yields on interest-earning assets, lower crediting rates on interest-bearing liabilities, and higher overall NIM. The contrarian read for CFO conversations: a December hike is not uniformly a headwind. It is a sorting mechanism that rewards the banks that made the right balance-sheet calls eighteen months ago, and it will make the deposit-mix conversation with boards more quantitative and less philosophical in Q1 2027.
---
### Client Conversation Hooks
1. **The December hike as a budget stress-test:** With a seventy-seven percent probability of a December ninth hike, does your client's 2027 NII budget have an explicit rate-scenario branch, and can the FP&A infrastructure re-run it fast enough to inform board presentations?
2. **Basel III Endgame capital relief is a treasury modeling event, not just a regulatory event:** The move from dual-stack to single standardized-approach calculation, plus the subsidiary-to-holding-company capital shift, requires the capital allocation and regulatory reporting engines to be rebuilt before 2027 implementation begins.
3. **Agentic AI ROI is real, but only for banks with clean data foundations:** The BCG nine-month transformation case is real, but it began with governed, integrated financial data. Ask your bank clients whether their current data architecture can actually support an agent deployment, or whether the data cleanup is the real project.

This is entirely new and directly relevant to bank CFO planning assumptions. 2. **The global bond selloff is at multi-decade extremes**: 30-year yields hit their highest since 2004 mid-week before stabilizing today, a specific threshold not previously surfaced. The bond selloff is simultaneously pressuring bank AFS portfolios and raising the long-end funding cost for term deposits and FHLB advances. 3. **Polymarket's October hike probability is now 64-65%**, materially up from the 54% covered yesterday, driven by nonfarm payrolls (October 2) and September CPI (October 14) as the next two catalysts. 4. **The August PCE release drops Tuesday, September 30**, with the BEA simultaneously releasing the Q2 GDP third estimate; this dual release creates compounded scenario risk for CFO planning assumptions over the long weekend. 5. **The Basel III re-proposal comment period closed June 18, 2026**: agencies are now in the comment-analysis phase. The key new angle is that the March 2026 reproposal explicitly introduces a **separate, lighter-touch approach for regional and smaller banks** distinct from the GSIBs -- directly relevant to the super-regional cohort. 6. **Agentic AI deployment sequencing**: BCG's June 2026 executive paper establishes the authoritative sequence -- AP automation first, then close, then FP&A refresh -- and the data is clear that timeline is driven by data readiness, not AI technology maturity. This is the buying-pattern angle: where banks should be spending budget first. 7. **The US-China AI and trade talks** at UNGA level, with a trade truce extension of three to six months possible, are a geopolitical variable moderating tariff-driven cost-push inflation -- directly feeding bank macro planning scenarios.
---
**WRITTEN BRIEFING**
---
# Finance Pulse | Friday, September 25, 2026
**Bottom line: A potential US-Iran deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz is today's single biggest CFO planning variable -- if oil reverses from $107, the entire inflation trajectory and October hike math shifts, requiring banks to immediately rebuild their rate scenario stacks.**
---
## Top Takeaways
1. Oil declined today as US and Iranian negotiators explored a phased deal that would see Tehran reopen the Strait of Hormuz, while a global bond selloff that drove yields to multi-decade highs stabilized in Asia as oil snapped a two-day surge. For bank CFOs, a sustained oil reversal from current levels would directly compress the headline PCE reading arriving Tuesday, the single most consequential data point before October 28.
2. The bond selloff deepened this week with 30-year yields hitting their highest since 2004, an acute pressure point for banks holding long-duration AFS securities and for those refinancing FHLB advances or term deposits at elevated wholesale rates.
3. With the next nonfarm payrolls report due October 2 and September CPI on October 14, these releases represent the key near-term catalysts that could shift the current implied probability on a 25 basis point increase in October. As of Thursday's close, Polymarket shows a 65% chance of a 25 basis point hike at the October meeting versus 35% for no change.
---
## Three Key Themes
### 1. The Hormuz-Inflation Feedback Loop *(New)* The Iran geopolitical development is not just an oil story. Persistent inflation, with headline PCE projected at 3.7% and core at 3.4% for 2026 amid energy price shocks from geopolitical tensions, import tariffs, and robust AI-driven capital spending, has prompted the hawkish shift under Chair Kevin Warsh. A phased Hormuz reopening would directly attack the energy component of that inflation projection. Bank CFOs who built their Q4 2026 NIM forecasts around a 4.1% terminal rate must now hold parallel scenarios -- one in which energy disinflation cools October hike conviction, and one in which it does not.
### 2. The Long-End Yield Problem Is Now a Balance Sheet Problem *(Evolving)* Prior episodes noted the 10-year crossing 5%; today the story has moved from the 10-year to the 30-year, which is a different instrument with different implications. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell for a third straight session as Treasury yields at multidecade highs continued to weigh on the most cyclical parts of the market. For bank controllers and treasurers, 30-year yields at 2004 levels mean that any AFS portfolio with duration extension in the three-to-ten-year belly now carries unrealized losses that have not fully appeared in prior stress scenarios. AOCI drag is the mechanism, and it directly constrains the capital ratio math the controller must report at Q3 close.
### 3. Basel III Reproposal: The Regional Bank Carve-Out Is the Underreported Story *(New)* The March 2026 proposals revisit Basel III Endgame for the largest firms, introduce a separate approach for regional and smaller banks, and revise the GSIB surcharge framework. The comment period closed June 18. Agencies are now analyzing responses. Overall, bank capital requirements are expected to decrease across the industry due to lower minimum risk weights, less conservative methodologies, lower buffers and surcharges, and a narrower application of the market risk framework. For PNC, Truist, U.S. Bancorp, and the rest of the super-regional cohort, this tiered architecture is the most favorable regulatory development in years -- but it also raises a finance transformation demand signal: if capital requirements ease, banks will redirect compliance investment toward growth infrastructure, not further defensive capital builds.
---
## Banking Finance-Function Metrics
**NIM and Deposit Costs:** As of market close on September 24, futures markets are pricing an increase to about 4.3% by December and roughly 4.8% by September 2027, extending expectations for tighter policy following the Federal Reserve's recent rate increase. This forward path matters acutely for deposit repricing. Banks that locked in lower deposit costs in H1 2026 when cuts were the base case are now facing a repricing curve moving in the wrong direction. PCE measures continue to show more persistent annual price pressure than recent headline CPI momentum.
**Wages and Operating Cost:** In August, hourly wages increased 3.30% year-over-year and at a 2.75% annualized pace over the past three months. Wage growth has moderated from the roughly 4.00% annual pace recorded in October 2025, but wages continue to advance. For bank efficiency ratios, moderating but still-positive real wage growth means the cost base is not yet deflating even as workloads rise.
**Q3 Close Timing:** Tuesday's simultaneous release of August PCE and the Q2 GDP third estimate creates a compounded data event landing exactly as Q3 books close. August PCE inflation arrives September 30 at 8:30 AM ET. The release also includes revised prior data and the simultaneous GDP release.
---
## Regulatory Radar
**Basel III Reproposal -- Comment Analysis Phase:** On March 19, 2026, the Federal Reserve Board, the OCC and the FDIC jointly issued three Notices for Proposed Rulemaking, rescinding the 2023 Basel III Endgame proposal. Although the proposals may relieve certain capital pressures, the 2026 capital rules also add complexity and will require careful implementation. The finalization timeline means banks should not defer re-engineering their regulatory capital calculation infrastructure; the comment period has closed, and implementation planning can now begin in earnest.
**US-China Trade Truce:** The talks at UNGA focused on delivering on what has been agreed by lead negotiators. A trade truce extension is possible, with US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer saying a three-to-six-month extension is possible. For bank CFOs, a truce extension moderates tariff-driven cost-push inflation in their macro scenarios.
---
## AI in Finance: Adoption, Vendors, and Buying Patterns
The clearest new development today is the emergence of a documented, empirically grounded **deployment sequence** that is now shaping where finance technology budgets are actually flowing.
Across organizations deploying autonomous accounts payable automation and agentic AI in production, several patterns have emerged: AP automation typically deploys first due to high volume, clear rules, and measurable baseline metrics; reconciliation and close automation follows as AP success builds organizational confidence; FP&A forecast refresh automates once operational data quality improves through AP and close automation.
This sequencing is not a vendor preference -- it is a data-readiness constraint. A single workflow such as AP or close typically reaches full value in four to six months. A portfolio of agents across the CFO office reaches full value in twelve to eighteen months. Timeline is driven by data readiness and change management, not by the underlying AI technology.
**CFO-to-agenda connection:** For bank finance leaders evaluating AI spend, this means the RFP question is not "which vendor has the best FP&A AI" but "is our AP and close data infrastructure clean enough to support an agent?" Banks that cannot answer yes are buying sequence wrong and will face the remediation costs that come with skipping steps.
Gartner predicts 40% of enterprise applications will be integrated with task-specific AI agents by end of 2026, up from less than 5% in 2025. In finance specifically, Deloitte's Q4 2025 CFO Signals survey found that 54% of CFOs say integrating AI agents into their finance departments will be a top transformation priority in 2026, and 87% believe AI will be extremely or very important to finance operations this year.
**Treasury-specific deployment:** Treasury functions are using agentic AI to optimize cash positioning across bank accounts and currencies, automate payment scheduling based on real-time liquidity data, and flag anomalies in cash flows that traditional reconciliation would miss until month-end. For bank treasurers managing intraday liquidity under a rapidly shifting rate environment, this is a capability with immediate ROI -- not a future-state vision.
**Governance as the scaling mechanism:** Governance is not a constraint on agentic AI; it is what allows it to scale. For bank CFOs whose finance AI governance frameworks are underdeveloped, this is the blocking item for budget approval. The vendors winning bank mandates are those with immutable audit logs, role-based permissions, and human-in-the-loop controls built in -- not bolted on.
---
## CFO Agenda, FP&A, and Transformation Signals
**The weekend scenario-planning imperative:** Tuesday's PCE and GDP dual release, arriving five weeks before the October 28 FOMC meeting, means finance teams should enter the weekend with pre-built scenario branches: (a) oil disinflation materializes and October hike probability retreats toward 40%, (b) PCE comes in above 3.7% and probability surges above 70%, and (c) GDP revision surprises to the downside, introducing recession scenario hedging. Each branch carries different NIM, provisioning, and capital planning implications.
**Finance transformation demand force:** The convergence of the 30-year yield shock, the dual September 30 data release, and an unresolved rate path is exactly the environment that exposes the inadequacy of static annual budgets. Banks without dynamic, driver-based planning models are flying blind into Q4. This is the most direct client conversation opener for finance transformation work: the current environment makes the cost of underpowered FP&A infrastructure visible and measurable.
---
## Contrarian Insight
The banking industry and its advisors are framing the Basel III regional bank carve-out as a straightforward capital relief story. It is not. The changes could materially affect bank capital requirements, profitability, product and service offerings, and long-term growth strategies, and the 2026 capital rules add complexity and will require careful implementation. The tiered architecture introduces a new definitional boundary between GSIB treatment and regional bank treatment that banks must now model, report, and govern. Super-regionals that assume the lighter-touch regime means less infrastructure investment are misjudging the complexity of operating at the boundary. The finance function investment case actually strengthens, not weakens, under the new framework.
---
## Three Client Conversation Hooks
1. **"If the Hormuz deal closes over the weekend, how quickly can your FP&A team rebuild the rate scenario that drives your Q4 NIM guidance?"** -- tests planning agility and scenario infrastructure maturity.
2. **"Your 30-year Treasury AFS exposure -- what does your AOCI sensitivity look like at yields last seen in 2004, and how does that constrain your Q3 capital ratio narrative?"** -- surfaces a balance sheet risk that has moved faster than most bank models anticipated.
3. **"When you evaluate AI for finance, are you buying in deployment sequence -- starting with AP and close data quality -- or are you skipping to FP&A agents on a data foundation that cannot yet support them?"** -- repositions the AI conversation from vendor selection to transformation readiness.
